newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: POLL-TRUST IN CZECH PM APPEARS TO HAVE BOTTOMED OUT.
newsitem.headline: POLL-TRUST IN CZECH PM APPEARS TO HAVE BOTTOMED OUT.

text.p: Trust in Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, on the wane since the beginning of the year, appears to have bottomed out, a public opinion poll released on Wednesday showed.

The survey, taken by the private polling agency STEM during the first week of July, said Czechs' trust in the PM remained at an all-time low of 31 percent, but the figure was unchanged from a poll taken in June.

Soon after the 1989 revolution which ousted the Communist government, Klaus won acclaim for a rapid voucher-based privatisation scheme that he led, which transferred thousands of companies into private hands.

But the economy, once considered a model of reform, has been hit recently by a huge trade deficit blamed largely on poor corporate restructuring. That led to fierce speculative attacks on the value of the crown, forcing the central bank to float the currency on May 27, letting it fall even further.

Klaus narrowly averted being ousted at the beginning of June, cutting a last minute deal with an independent deputy to squeak out the confidence vote for his three-party cabinet and its package of tough austerity measures 101-99 in the lower house of parliament.
As economic problems grew -- bringing to light many of the stumbling blocks the fledgling economy still has to face up to -- Klaus's rating eroded from 51 percent in January to its current level.

However, Klaus's foil on the Czech political scene, President Vaclav Havel, who acts more as a philosophical balancing wheel for the country than a political animal, maintains the broad trust which brought him to power after the revolution.
The STEM survey showed that trust in the former dissident playwright turned President remains solid at 66 percent.

Havel frequently battles for the soul of Czech reforms with his long-time right- wing economist prime minister, Vaclav Klaus -- Havel preaching his gospel of the civic society, while Klaus espouses individualism.

A president who has clashed with Klaus over priorities for the transformation of Czech society, Havel is not a member of any political party. He is elected by parliament and is not directly involved in party politics.
